name: Testicular sun / red light exposure

card.summary: Shining sunlight or red light on the testes in hopes of higher testosterone; a fringe idea with no human trials behind it.
card.aka: testicle sunning, red light on balls
card.note: No studies found; the testes are normally kept cooler than the body, and heat is associated with reduced sperm quality.

quick.overview:
Testicular sun or red light exposure is a fringe practice in which men expose the scrotum to sunlight or to red or near-infrared lamps, believing it will raise testosterone or improve sperm. It circulates in biohacking and health-influencer circles and occasionally on looksmaxxing forums.
No human trials were found testing it for testosterone, fertility or appearance. The surrounding science concerns two separate things: red-light therapy for other conditions, and the well-documented sensitivity of sperm production to heat.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say light stimulates Leydig cells or mitochondria in testicular tissue, which they associate with testosterone production. Red-light therapy (photobiomodulation) is studied for pain and wound problems, but testicular effects are not documented.
quick.risks: The scrotum keeps the testes a few degrees below core temperature, and higher temperatures are reported to impair spermatogenesis. Lamps or sun can add heat and skin exposure risks such as burns. Light therapy devices are cleared by the FDA only for specific uses, and none are cleared for this one.

lead: Testicular sun or red light exposure, nicknamed "testicle tanning" in media coverage, is a practice in which men expose the scrotum to sunlight or to red or near-infrared lamps in the hope of raising testosterone. Proponents link higher testosterone with the things many men want to see in the mirror: more muscle, leaner body composition, more energy to train and a more masculine overall look, so the practice is discussed in biohacking circles and occasionally in looksmaxxing hormone-optimisation threads.[1][2][8]

The idea drew wide attention in April 2022 when Andrew McGovern, a personal trainer, promoted infrared light on the scrotum on Tucker Carlson's Fox News special The End of Men, where he called it "bromeotherapy".[3] Proponents also point to a 1939 study of a handful of hospitalised men and to a small unpublished conference study.[4]

Red and near-infrared light applied to the body is studied as photobiomodulation for conditions such as pain, wound healing and hair loss, and a 2023 paper examined photobiomodulation and human sperm function in the lab.[1][5][6] Urologists quoted in media say they know of no data showing that light on the testes raises testosterone, and they note the testes are normally kept cooler than the body, with heat associated with reduced sperm quality.[3][4][7]
infobox: Sunlight or red/near-infrared lamp on the scrotum
1939 five-man UV study; small unpublished study [4]

paras: Practitioners describe exposing the scrotal area to sunlight outdoors or to a red or near-infrared panel for short sessions. The reasoning offered is that light reaches testicular tissue and stimulates testosterone-producing cells.[3][4] Skeptic magazine's review notes that despite the nickname, the red-light version is not tanning at all, since red light does not tan skin; the term comes from the sunlight version and from the media shorthand.[4]

A related variant, perineal sunning, is promoted on social media as an ancient Taoist practice. The review describes an Instagram wellness influencer presenting the perineum as a gateway for solar energy and claiming benefits ranging from libido and sleep to focus and hormone regulation, and notes that the post offered no scientific evidence.[4]

The appeal of the practice rests on what testosterone does. Endocrinology references describe it as anabolic, increasing muscle mass and strength and bone density; at puberty it broadens the shoulders, expands the rib cage, deepens the voice and drives beard and body hair, and together with growth hormone it remodels the jaw, brow, chin and nose.[8] Low testosterone is associated with fat accumulation, and in older men maintaining normal levels was associated with less visceral fat.[8] Proponents of testicular light therefore frame it as a route to a leaner, more muscular, more energetic look. That chain depends on the first step, light raising testosterone, which proponents assert and which has not been demonstrated.

Most testosterone in men is made by Leydig cells in the testes under the control of luteinizing hormone from the pituitary, with feedback through the hypothalamus.[8][7] Proponents suggest light acts directly on this tissue, and some invoke mitochondria; urologists respond that the testes are internal organs that light does not reach.[3]

Proponents cite a 1939 study by Abraham Myerson and Rudolph Neustadt of Boston State Hospital, published in The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology. Skeptic's review describes it as involving five hospitalised depressed men, using ultraviolet light rather than red light or sunlight, and measuring androsterone, a testosterone metabolite, not testosterone itself. Androsterone excretion reportedly rose from 70 to 155 units after chest exposure and to 205 after genital exposure, an increase smaller than the popular claims of a tripling, and most men developed marked skin redness.[4] Inverse quotes UCLA urologist Jesse Mills describing the same idea as tracing to a 1939 study of about eight men without a control group that was never replicated.[3]

A second cited source is a small conference study by Andrea Fagiolini in men with low sexual desire, which reportedly found testosterone rising from 2.3 to 3.6 ng/mL after sessions under a UV-filtered light box and was not published in a peer-reviewed journal.[4]

The practice reached mainstream audiences through the April 2022 Fox News special, after which many outlets published expert reactions.[3][4] Host Tucker Carlson tied the topic to claims about falling testosterone in men; Inverse reports that guest McGovern said there was "so much data" behind it.[3][4]

Photobiomodulation applies low-power lasers or LEDs delivering red and near-infrared light to tissue. Its history includes Niels Finsen's red-light work, recognised with the 1903 Nobel Prize, and Hungarian surgeon Endre Mester's laser experiments, published from 1967, in which hair regrew faster on treated mice.[1] The accepted candidate mechanism is absorption by cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria.[1]

Reviews describe evidence as mixed: oral mucositis and breast-cancer-related lymphedema are among the better-supported uses, many pain conditions have tentative support, and androgenic alopecia trials have given mixed results, with one 2017 review finding improvement in most trials. Penetration is limited, with only a small fraction of visible red light reaching a couple of millimetres of tissue in one example given.[1] A 2025 consensus paper in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology addresses clinical application of the technique.[6]

The scrotum holds the testes about two or three degrees Celsius below core body temperature, roughly 35 versus 37 degrees, using the cremaster muscle, the dartos fascia and venous networks around the spermatic cord, and higher temperatures affect spermatogenesis.[2] Another reference describes sperm production as impeded above roughly 36.7 degrees Celsius.[7]

Urologist Ashley Winter wrote on Twitter that there is no data on testicle tanning, said the testes cannot be tanned, and said red light might at most reduce redness of scrotal skin without reaching the testes or stimulating testosterone production.[3] Jesse Mills noted that testosterone levels can swing by around 100 points in a day, so a later test can look higher without any treatment, and that heat can harm sperm and fertility. He also said men with low-normal levels and symptoms who feel dismissed by medicine may be drawn to unproven remedies.[3]

The Skeptic review, by physician Harriet Hall, reports that urologists found no scientific evidence for the claim, that the Cleveland Clinic found insufficient evidence for most red light therapy uses and none for raising testosterone, and that a study of full-body red light in athletes found no change in testosterone.[4] Another physician quoted there, Joe Schwarcz, strongly criticised the claims, and researcher Edzard Ernst wrote on his blog that he was perplexed by perineal sunning.[4]

Because testicular heat is associated with impaired spermatogenesis, heat from lamps or direct sun is a concern for fertility.[2][7][3] Skin burns are a general risk of heat or ultraviolet exposure to sensitive skin; in the 1939 study most participants developed marked redness.[4] Light therapy devices cleared by the FDA are cleared for specific uses. Wikipedia's photobiomodulation article records that the FDA obtained a permanent injunction in 2015 against one device maker that marketed lasers as treating over 200 diseases, and that its owner later pleaded guilty to misbranding conspiracy charges.[1]

Related research includes a 2023 laboratory study of photobiomodulation and human sperm function, red-light therapy trials for other conditions, and studies of heat effects on spermatogenesis, but none tests light applied to the testes for testosterone.[5][1][2]

Testicular light sits alongside other hormone-optimisation and wellness trends discussed in biohacking spaces, including whole-body red light panels, outdoor sun exposure and other claimed testosterone boosters. Skeptic magazine groups perineal sunning with other wellness fads such as cupping and detox regimens, and lists testimonials, distrust of authority and a sense of empowerment among reasons such practices spread.[4]

timeline.event: Niels Finsen receives the Nobel Prize for light therapy, an early landmark in phototherapy.[1]
Myerson and Neustadt report androsterone changes in five hospitalised men after ultraviolet exposure.[4]
Endre Mester publishes low-power laser findings that founded photobiomodulation.[1]
A permanent US injunction is granted against a laser-device maker that marketed devices for 200-plus diseases.[1]
Andrew McGovern promotes the practice on a Fox News special in April, prompting urologist responses.[3][4]
Skeptic magazine publishes a review of testicle tanning and perineal sunning (November).[4]
A laboratory study examines photobiomodulation effects on human sperm function.[5]

lore.intro: Proponents in biohacking and some looksmaxxing circles discuss light on the testes as a low-cost testosterone aid, and media coverage since 2022 has recorded both the claims and clinicians' responses.[3][4]

claims.claim: Sunlight or red light on the testes raises testosterone.
claims.believers: Proponents say light stimulates testicular cells and boosts hormone output, citing a 1939 study and a small conference study.[4]
claims.experts: Urologists quoted in media say there is no data and that light does not reach the testes; the 1939 study had no control group and was not replicated.[3][4]

claims.claim: The 1939 study showed a large testosterone boost.
claims.believers: Popular summaries describe the study as showing testosterone rising severalfold after light exposure.[4]
claims.experts: Skeptic's review says the study used ultraviolet light on five hospitalised men and measured androsterone, a metabolite, with a smaller rise than popularly claimed.[4]

claims.believers: Advocates say light therapy supports sperm and testicular health.
claims.experts: No human trial has tested this by applying light to the testes; separately, heat is reported to impair spermatogenesis.[2][7] A 2023 lab study examined photobiomodulation and sperm function.[5]

claims.claim: Perineal sunning draws in solar energy and balances hormones.
claims.believers: Wellness influencers present it as an ancient Taoist practice that boosts libido, sleep and focus.[4]
claims.experts: Skeptic's review notes that no scientific evidence was offered and that physicians who commented were critical.[4]

claims.claim: Red light therapy generally is a proven healing tool.
claims.believers: Supporters cite benefits in pain and tissue repair.
claims.experts: Photobiomodulation evidence is mixed, with tentative support for some conditions and weaker results for others.[1]

claims.claim: Testosterone readings go up after a session, proving it works.
claims.believers: Some users report a higher blood test after starting.
claims.experts: Mills noted that testosterone can swing by about 100 points within a day, so a later reading can be higher without any intervention.[3]

claims.claim: Heating the testicles with lamps is harmless.
claims.believers: Some users describe short sessions as comfortable.
claims.experts: Mills warned that heat can harm sperm, and reference texts link higher scrotal temperature to impaired spermatogenesis.[3][2]

chain: Light is applied to the scrotum

angle.text: The practice is used by men who want higher testosterone for a leaner, more muscular physique and better training capacity. The link from light to testosterone is the proponents' claim; the link from testosterone to muscle and body composition is well established in endocrinology.
